av3zdxYvCp8.tx: For over four decades, Walter Cavanagh held a truly credit-worthy record: the most credit cards held by one person. What began as a bet between friends led him to open over 1,400 cards, ranging from traditional bank-issued to those from airlines, gas stations, and even ice cream shops. Most people have far fewer credit cards. While useful for secure purchasing, handling emergencies, and building credit scores, credit cards can make it difficult to avoid overspending. Globally, the outstanding credit card debt exceeds trillions of dollars. And this is no accident. Credit card companies intentionally design these systems to encourage spending and lock you into a cycle of interest and fees. So, how can you avoid their most common traps? It starts with card selection. Lenders often aggressively advertise perks like cash back, travel miles, and discounts. But these offers only seem generous. In reality, only a small portion of cardholders actually benefit— those who pay off their entire balance every month. But according to one survey, 46% of American cardholders carry a revolving balance. For these users, the cost of interest and fees almost always exceeds the value of rewards. If you think you may fall into this category, financial experts recommend getting a card with the lowest annual percentage rate, or APR. This number is essentially the cost of borrowing money from the credit card company. You pay that cost through interest charges, which kick in as soon as you carry any balance past a statement due date. While APRs are listed as yearly rates, for most cards, interest accrues daily. For example, a card with a 35% APR charges about 0.095% interest per day. So a revolving balance of $1,000 would accumulate approximately $29 in interest over a month. Meanwhile, a card with a lower APR, say 18%, would charge about $15 in interest during the same period. This difference can add up over time. If you were to make a $50 monthly payment towards that $1,000 balance, the card with the higher APR would take an extra $325 and an extra seven months to pay off. And interest fees can be even more complicated. If you carry a balance and actively use a card, new purchases start accruing interest immediately, even if you pay off those purchases before the statement date. In other words, once you start to carry a balance, it’s much more difficult to avoid interest charges going forward. And even after a bill is fully paid, you might still get one more charge, something called residual interest, for the days between your statement and payment date. Low APR cards are the best option for minimizing these interest charges; however, be wary of cards that offer exceptionally low APR for an introductory period. These flashy offers can mask things like complicated fee structures, steep late charges, and high default APRs that kick in once the introductory period ends. While many countries require companies to disclose these conditions, they're often buried in the fine print. Payment structures can also be confusing. For example, many people mistake the minimum payment as the standard or even recommended amount to pay. In reality, it typically only covers interest, fees, and a small percentage of the balance. As a result, sticking to just the minimum payment can make even a low balance of $1,000 take over 18 years to pay off. Paying the full card balance each month is the best way to avoid fees and actually benefit from rewards. But it's not always possible. So what should you do if you find yourself in credit card debt? The first step is to assess your finances and create a repayment plan. If the debt is on a high APR card, transferring your balance to a lower APR card may help. Just be sure to check for balance transfer fees. If you’re juggling debt on multiple cards, it may be tempting to pay off the lowest balance first. However, the most financially efficient strategy will always be to put any extra money towards the card with the highest APR, regardless of balance. The key is to chip away one card at a time— just don’t be like Walter and open a thousand more in the meantime.

JjhrN0FcHpM.tx: Order, order! Who do we have on the stand today? Queen Victoria... wasn’t she the definition of straight laced? Indeed, Your Honor. Throughout her 63-year reign, she was a tireless model of morality and restraint. So much so that the 19th century is popularly called the “Victorian Age” and is still associated with those very qualities. Unfortunately, this era is also associated with rigid gender roles, deep class divisions, and the subjugation of colonized peoples— all reinforced by Queen Victoria's so-called virtues. Her moralistic approach to monarchy was more concerned with making the British Empire look like a big happy family than actually helping anyone inside it. I guess appearances can be deceiving. In her defense, Your Honor, Victoria came to the throne at the tender age of 18 and faced immediate pressure to restore public faith in the crown. The previous two kings had been drinkers, womanizers, and gamblers. Meanwhile, Victoria was expected to serve as the country's moral compass during the dizzying changes brought by industrialization. Well, she certainly got her chance. Her reign coincided with the birth of mass media, giving her the power to exert immense cultural influence. In newspapers, she appeared as the perfect wife to her beloved Prince Albert. Press images of her pure white wedding dress started a fashion trend that continues to this day. And front pages featuring their family’s idyllic Christmas celebrations set a new standard for middle class society. Specifically a standard that shamed any family who couldn’t afford a picture-perfect holiday. She had to cultivate the image of a dutiful wife and dedicated mother to meet popular expectations— even though her relationship with her children was sometimes stormy. Besides, she wasn't entirely traditional. While religious leaders and some doctors argued against using pain medication during childbirth, Victoria made the practice socially acceptable by using anesthesia during the births of two of her children. And she publicly supported the entry of women into the field of nursing. She also opposed giving women the right to vote, and believed they should focus on their household responsibilities instead of politics. She viewed her position as a powerful woman as an accident of birth, not as a model for her gender. Well, that's not exactly the most inspiring message. Victoria simply mirrored and reinforced larger cultural trends; she didn’t create them. Besides, her public persona was the only reliable tool she had for affecting change in Britain. As a constitutional monarch, the Queen was expected to act on the advice of her Prime Minister. And while some of the ministers she worked with during her reign actively encouraged her to shape Britain’s politics, others, like Lord John Russell, dismissed her ideas. Yet, when Russell’s government failed to address the Irish Potato Famine, Victoria received the blame. In fact, she’s still known as the “Famine Queen” to this day. That moniker may have more to do with her measly personal donation of £2,000 to famine relief, which was less than 1% of her annual stipend. And when the Ottoman sultan wanted to donate £10,000, the British Embassy talked him down to 1,000 so his generosity wouldn’t make Victoria look bad! Just like everything in her reign, Victoria cared more about her reputation than her people. She was actually very aware of how difficult her subjects’ lives were. As a child, her mother took her on tours around the UK to see how people lived. And as an adult, she read authors like Charles Dickens to better understand the lower classes. She backed social reforms like the establishment of state-funded public schools and the Public Health Act of 1875, which aimed to improve sanitation and living conditions. While I'm sure those policies helped her domestic subjects, Victoria frequently ignored her countless more international citizens. She believed that Britain should be an empire over which the sun never set, meaning she completely supported colonial expansion. It’s true— Victoria was a product of her time and believed in Britain’s imperial destiny. But she was also interested in learning about the various cultures within her empire, developing close relationships with Sarah Forbes Bonnetta, a formerly enslaved West African woman, and with Abdul Karim, an Indian secretary who taught her Hindustani. Victoria and Albert were also known abolitionists who supported deploying the Royal Navy to combat West Africa's illegal slave trade. Noble efforts, no doubt. But Victoria did nothing to counter the violent oppression and paternalistic racism that marked Britain's colonial expansion. These colonies’ inhabitants were frequently mistreated, and they could only advance so far in their country’s government, even if they were British educated. Let's not sugarcoat it. Under her watch, British forces brutally crushed uprisings in South Asia and Africa, looted resources, and enforced racial hierarchies that lasted long after her reign. Doesn’t exactly sound like a “big happy family” to me. Queen Victoria might have tried to hold her empire to a higher standard, but should we judge leaders by their ideals or their outcomes? These are the questions we have to ask when putting history on trial.

tu6tF-lVDJI.tx: Can we eat our way to a stronger democracy? (Laughter) Normally, when we talk about strengthening democracy, we talk voting, town halls, civic engagement. All of that matters. But I'd like to suggest something unexpected. Food. Food may be as essential to a strong democracy if we accept two simple ideas. First, democracy relies upon us knowing each other. Being able to talk to one another. Understanding that disagreement does not make someone an enemy. And second, food is one of our last common denominators. No matter your race, income or religion, we all have a cuisine. And those cuisines are more than just their ingredients. They're collections of stories, histories, values, memories. When we start to learn something about one another's cuisine, we often discover something deeper. We are not as different from each other as we think. That’s the bet we made in 2016 with Breaking Bread, Breaking Barriers. Twelve immigrant and native-born communities came together in partnership with the Reading Terminal Market, the city and local organizations. We cooked together, ate together, talked through facilitated dialogue, almost entirely about food, over dinner with strangers we may otherwise never meet. Folks sharing recipes on how chicken is fried in their respective cultures. Trading stories about Sunday night dinner traditions with extended family. Talking about those food-centered holidays we all celebrate. Over the years, nearly 400 Philadelphians took part in four different versions, and this year, for our 250th anniversary, over 700, across seven Philly neighborhoods, are taking part in a version that has catalyzed a city-wide conversation on citizenship, at a time when that word divides more often than it unites. What I've witnessed over the years has been profound. War-weary Syrian refugees being welcomed over dinner by their new neighbors in Northeast Philly as if they'd known each other for decades. A single mother, isolated during the pandemic, sharing through a virtual dinner with strangers that this was the first human interaction she'd had in nearly a year since the pandemic began beyond her immediate family. And a 12-year-old boy, standing unsolicited in a room full of adults to simply state: if more people took the time to learn about each other, the world would be a richer place. The idea is simple but replicable. Where we differ, lean in. Share a recipe with a neighbor. Tell them what it means to you, who passed it down and what memories it evokes. Chances are they'll start telling you a surprisingly similar story. And from there, you've just created the possibility that democracy relies upon most: a connection with those we perceive as different. Now let's get some lunch and build democracy for the next 250 years. Thank you. (Cheers and applause)

On average, users stuck with a single task for 40 seconds, down from 75 seconds, measured just five years earlier. This doesn’t necessarily mean our attention spans are fundamentally getting shorter. Rather, in today’s world, our attention is being pulled in more directions than ever before. This can make finding focus— for work, school, and even the things we love— feel almost impossible. Thankfully, there are ways we can improve and better protect our attention spans, both online and off. Our brains are constantly receiving a flood of information, from sensory input to environmental cues to internal thoughts. Filtering through it all relies on several brain regions. The prefrontal cortex helps us decide what to pay attention to, while the parietal cortex shines a mental flashlight on that prioritized stream of information while ignoring the rest. The challenge of sustained attention is keeping that flashlight focused in one place. The brain is continuously monitoring all these competing signals. And it redirects your focus if anything is flagged as particularly novel, unexpected, or emotionally charged— whether it’s a knock on the door, a notification, or even a passing thought. This ability to constantly scan our environments and quickly refocus was key for human survival. So, while frustrating, getting distracted is inevitable. And our baseline ability to manage distractions can vary based on factors like genetics and brain differences. But no matter your starting point, there are ways to improve your ability to stay focused. First, tasks that appropriately challenge you tend to hold your attention best. For example, you might focus better when working on a more difficult, intricately patterned puzzle than an easier one. Of course, we don’t always have a choice in what needs to get done. In these situations, it’s helpful to remember that if focusing feels like work, that's because it is. In fact, some researchers theorize that attention is a limited resource. When you start focusing on something, this resource is at its highest, but it depletes over time, leading to more mistakes and increasing the chance you’ll be distracted. Multitasking only increases the demand for this resource, exhausting attentional stores more quickly. That's why focusing on one task and intentionally building in breaks can be helpful. Studies even show a momentary break, to get a snack or just zone out, can reset this attentional resource. And this strategy may be extra beneficial when studying or practicing a new skill. During breaks, our minds replay the neural activity patterns of what you just learned, helping to solidify the memory for the long term. Speaking of studying, stress, sleepiness, and poor mood can all weaken our ability to block out distractions. So activities that reduce stress, like exercising, chatting with friends, or getting a good night’s sleep, also make it easier to stay focused. And nature may offer an extra boost. In one study, a 15-minute walk outdoors led to greater improvements in lab-based attention tasks than the same walk indoors. Another effective strategy is mindfulness meditation. This practice is all about staying in the present moment through exercises like spending 12 minutes focusing on the sensations of breathing, which can help train your attention over time. But before you go take a walk, grab a snack, or learn to meditate, there’s something much easier you can do right in this moment: get rid of distractions. It’s impossible to remove every distraction, after all, our own wandering minds are often the biggest culprits. But one recent survey estimated that Americans now check their phones around 200 times a day. The distractions on our screens are designed to grab and hold attention. So, remember to be kind to yourself. While we can’t always control every factor that pulls at our attention, finding a quiet environment, closing extra tabs, and even blocking certain apps can give your brain the best chance at focusing in.

bHB5iiDDJ-s.tx: In March 2024, US veterinarians were facing down a mystery. On dairy farms in Texas and nearby states, cows were losing their appetite and producing thick, discolored milk. At the same time, cats on these farms were being diagnosed with an unknown neurological disease. For weeks, all their tests for common cattle diseases came back negative until lab results finally uncovered the culprit: influenza A subtype H5N1 — more commonly known as bird flu. This wasn’t the first time a virus adapted for birds infected non-avian animals. In fact, every human influenza pandemic on record has been linked to some strain of bird flu. So what is it about these viruses that makes them so frighteningly flexible? Of the four groups of flu viruses, all bird flus fall into group A. Within this group, the viruses are organized into subtypes defined by two viral proteins. Hemagglutinin binds to host cell receptors, allowing the virus to enter the cell and replicate. And neuraminidase helps those new viruses leave the cell. Currently, we’ve discovered 18 types of hemagglutinin and 11 types of neuraminidase, and different subtypes of influenza A use different combinations. For example, the combo of hemagglutinin 5 and neuraminidase 1 is called H5N1. These proteins are necessary for influenza A to enter and exit host cells, so they generally determine which animals a strain can infect. But birds, especially wild aquatic birds, have receptors for most known versions of these proteins, making them susceptible to nearly all combinations. Worse still, these waterfowl shed the virus through their feces into lakes and ponds, increasing the odds of infection for any bird using those bodies of water. And since the viruses don’t usually make these birds actively sick, they can act as reservoirs for disease— flying around and spreading their strain. Thankfully, humans are mostly safe from all these flus. We only have receptors for a few viral proteins, protecting us from most combinations. And while bird flus can sometimes bind to receptors in our airways, our more vulnerable receptors are deep in our lungs. This makes infection less likely and transmission less efficient compared to common human flus that target receptors in our nose and throat. Unfortunately, influenza has other tricks up its sleeves. Viruses have antigens— specific molecules that our immune system can recognize and attack to fight against an infection. But two processes are constantly changing these molecules and challenging our immune systems. The first is antigenic drift, where antigens change slowly over time due to random mutations. This makes it harder for immune systems to recognize the virus, but the process is relatively slow and trackable. In fact, we manage the antigenic drift of human flu by updating our flu shots every year. The much more sudden and potentially dangerous process is antigenic shift. This happens when two or more different influenza viruses meet inside a host and swap entire gene segments, instantly creating a new virus with all-new abilities— including the potential to bind to different receptors and infect different species. This is why bird flus are so concerning. Since birds are vulnerable to so many influenza A subtypes, they’re natural reservoirs for antigenic shifts. Consider our dairy farm mystery. While H5N1 used to infect mostly birds, in the past few years, it’s been found in over 70 mammal species, including cats, dairy cows, foxes, seals, and bears. Each new mammalian infection gives the virus more chances to drift or shift, potentially spilling over into humans, and igniting a pandemic. And since our immune systems aren’t trained to recognize avian influenza proteins, the effects of these viruses can be deadly. So, should we panic? Not yet. Despite the fact that influenza is ubiquitous in birds across the globe, bird flu infections in humans are still relatively rare. What's most important is to stay vigilant. Scientists are working around the clock to monitor ongoing viral evolution, test vaccines, and strengthen biosecurity. Everything could change with a single outbreak, ao the only way to win this viral arms race is to stay one flap ahead.

That is the very careful threading of the needle as we mark the 25th anniversary of 9/11, which is to pay respects to the people who were lost that day and to all of the families who, 25 years later, still feel greatly that empty place at every holiday, at every milestone. bw5tzcoEG88.tx: If you could wave a magic wand, what’s the one idea you’d most love to spread to other people’s minds? Through the power of language— carefully used— we can do just that. But what’s the most direct way of gifting an idea to an audience? Simply show it. Incorporating visuals can make a talk more powerful and convincing. Assuming you have your throughline and talk content, it's time to get this show on the road. In the 21st century, we can add to the spoken word with many technologies— pictures, illustrations, graphs, charts, animation, video, audio, and data. All can help explain your idea and make your talk visually interesting. But first, ask yourself whether you actually need visuals. At least a third of TED’s most-viewed talks don’t use slides at all. Slides move attention away from the speaker. If your talk relies on personal connection, humor, or stories, you may be better off speaking directly to the audience. For every speaker, the rule is simple: having no slides is better than having bad slides. But many talks benefit from strong visuals. Sometimes, the visuals make the talk a success. Key components of strong visuals fall into three categories: revelation, explanatory power, and aesthetic appeal. Revelation: The most obvious reason to use visuals is to show something hard to describe. Edith Widder was part of the team that first captured the giant squid on video. Her talk was built around that moment of revelation. When the creature appeared on screen, the audience nearly jumped out of its skin. Revelation doesn't have to be dramatic. Explain any background, prime the audience, and then let the visuals do their work. Run them full screen without adding anything. Explanatory power: Words and images often explain best together. Much of our world is imagined visually. To explain something new, showing and telling often works best. But the visual must fit the spoken message. Complicated slides can distract an audience. Limit each slide to one core idea. Multiple streams of information require mental energy to process. A speaker must direct attention so slides support, For graphs and charts, highlight the relevant parts. If comparing February and October rainfall, use colors to show the months. Don't cram everything onto one slide. Headlines with long bullet points often lose attention— turn bullets into separate slides, reduce phrases, or replace them with images. Even simple slides may steal your thunder. Instead of “A black hole is an object so massive that no light can escape,” try: “How black is a black hole?” Then deliver the information through speech; The slide teases curiosity and makes words more compelling. Visuals shouldn't communicate words your mouth can easily say. Use them to share what speech can’t: photographs, video, animation, or data. Screens can explain instantly what might take hours to describe. Aesthetic appeal: Nice-looking slides add power. Visually appealing slides can amplify a talk's impact. Hans Rosling is a TED speaker who excelled at this. “Here we go. Can you see there? It’s China. They’re moving — better health. They are improving. There, all the green Latin American countries. They are moving towards smaller families.” Not everyone can be a Hans Rosling, but every speaker can ask: are visuals essential for explaining my idea? And how can I combine them effectively with words? Once you plan your visuals, revisit your words and figure out how to turn them into a rewarding presentation. All these lessons should put you on your way to delivering a powerful talk— one that inspires, delights, and may even change the world.

BSdEiOYvKpE.tx: In 1930, as the Great Depression ravaged the United States, President Herbert Hoover made a bold economic decision. With the goal of supporting American farmers and manufacturers, he approved a sweeping 20% tax on all imported agricultural and industrial goods. He believed making foreign goods more expensive would encourage consumers to buy domestic, thus funneling cash into American businesses and creating more jobs. But Hoover's plan completely backfired. Other countries retaliated by taxing American goods, leading exports to fall and global trade to decline. In the end, this policy led American prices to spike and caused even more unemployment. These disastrous outcomes of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act were no surprise to the over 1,000 economists who publicly condemned the bill. But this wouldn’t be the last time a world leader was shocked by a tariff's consequences. So, what exactly is a tariff? A tariff is a tax an importer pays to bring foreign goods into a country. For example, if they import $1,000 worth of goods at a 10% tariff rate, they'll pay $100 to the government in addition to $1,000 to the seller. Foreign exporters could respond to a tariff by reducing their product’s price to keep an importer’s business. But if they don’t, importers bear this cost and then increase their prices so consumers will make up the difference. This may sound straightforward, but enacting a tariff kicks off a complicated economic chain reaction. So to keep things simple, let's look at some examples from just one country to explore some of the factors that make a tariff’s outcomes tricky to predict. First, tariffs can be applied to different countries at different rates. For example, in 2024, America had a 6% tariff on all wool entering the country. However, if that wool came from Mexico or South Korea, it would be tariff-free due to trade agreements. Meanwhile, importers getting wool from Russia could face a hefty 55.5% tariff. Policies like these might help domestic wool producers, or they might just encourage importers to buy from specific foreign producers. Things get even trickier when trying to predict how tariffs impact jobs. Sometimes the jobs they create come at a high cost. In 2018, the US imposed a tariff on washing machines that created 1,800 jobs and raised roughly $82 million in government revenue. However, it also increased the average price of washing machines by $86, costing consumers roughly $1.5 billion. This means consumers paid roughly $817,000 to create each of those jobs. In other cases, the jobs tariffs create come at the cost of existing jobs. In 2002, the Bush administration imposed tariffs as high as 30% on imported steel. Employment in US steel production had been decaying for decades, so by making foreign steel more expensive, the tariff sought to create new jobs for US steel manufacturers. Initially, the policy did slow down job loss. But since US steel still cost more than pre-tariff foreign steel, domestic industries that used this material had to increase their prices. This made their products less competitive internationally, where foreign manufacturers were still using cheap steel. Within a year of enacting the tariff, the US lost far more jobs in steel-related industries than they gained in steel-producing industries. Clearly, how other countries respond to tariffs is another big part of the ripple effect these policies have. One clear example comes from 2018, when the US attempted to address its trade deficit with China by taxing Chinese goods. While these tariffs protected domestic businesses and raised government revenue, they also set off a trade war. China retaliated by raising tariffs on US exporters, including farmers relying on Chinese markets for soybean sales. In the end, this led to higher prices for US consumers and a slight drop in America's GDP. Trade wars aren’t new. And even in the 18th and early 19th centuries, when certain tariffs did help struggling industries find their domestic footing, they were mostly used to raise government funds. But over the last 200 years, our global economy has become far more interdependent. Today, there are more manufacturing components being imported than ever before, many of which are used to make a wide variety of consumer goods. This complexity means that even a seemingly simple tariff can trigger a global chain reaction, creating more consequences than anyone can plan for.

JOs-q7rXqdk.tx: Your first job as a speaker is to build a trusting human bond with your audience. One excellent way to connect to an audience is to tell a story. Stories helped make us who we are. Really — evidence left behind from our ancient ancestors suggests that the human mind developed alongside human storytelling. Fire created a new magnet for bonding. Its warmth and flickering light drew people together after dark. This seems to have happened in every ancient culture over the last 300,000 years. And what did our ancestors do with this time together? In many cultures, one type of communal activity became very important: storytelling. Stories brought people from faraway places to the fireside. Stories about people who were alive and people who were dead, nearby and in distant lands. Stories sparked laughter, tension, and amazement. Stories also played an important role in helping expand people’s ability to imagine and to dream, and to understand the minds of others. Storytellers became important people within a community, and their listeners took information from the stories that changed how they behaved in the world. It's not just that we all love hearing stories. Stories probably helped shape how our minds share and receive information. So it's no surprise that many of the best talks are built around a story. The most basic way of breaking down a story is this: a character with a goal meets an unexpected obstacle. She tries to overcome that obstacle, which builds to a peak in the action. Finally, there’s some kind of resolution to the conflict. When it comes to sharing a story from the stage, remember four key things: 1. Base the story around a character your audience can empathize with. 2. Build tension, either through curiosity, relationship with other characters, or actual danger. 3. Offer the right level of detail. If there's not enough, the story won't come to life. If there's too much, it will get bogged down. And, 4. End with a satisfying conclusion, whether it’s funny, moving, or surprising. Some great talks are built around a single story. This can be really helpful for a speaker. The throughline is simply the plot of the story. If the story is about you, it can even create empathy in the audience. If your journey is exciting and easy to follow, this type of talk can work really well. But there's a trap here too. Remember, the goal is to give. Personal stories may entertain or interest an audience, or make the speaker feel really good about themselves, but they don’t necessarily give the audience something they can walk away with; a new way of understanding things, actionable information, context, hope. And that’s a real shame. The key is to link together the important moments of your story in a way that can be meaningful to someone else. Otherwise, it may sound like you're just rambling or speaking for the sake of hearing yourself talk. But, if the journey reveals something powerful you have learned, and if each step in your journey is revealed with humility and honesty and vulnerability, it is a journey we will gladly take with you. There is one other piece that is absolutely essential if you’re going to tell your own story: it has to be true. This may seem obvious, but sometimes speakers are tempted to exaggerate or even make a story up entirely. Stories can have such a big impact that some speakers are tempted to bend the truth. But even small exaggerations can quickly destroy your reputation. It's not worth the risk. 5jPCAlE0z7I.tx: >> In the mid-20th century, the first scuba technology allowed deep-sea divers in the Mediterranean to reach previously impossible depths. And after descending into the mesophotic zone, an ocean region spanning 30 to 150 m, these aquanauts made a remarkable discovery. Up to 90 m below the surface, where sometimes only 0.1% of surface sunlight can reach, they found a forest of huge kelps, over twice the size of a giraffe. Today, kelps are known to be the largest marine plants, and there had already been talk of such giants being pulled up from enormous depths in the late 19th century. But following the Mediterranean discovery, fishermen, naval officers, and scientists began dredging up more massive mesophotic kelps in the Philippine Sea and off the coasts of Brazil, Australia, and North America. There were even claims of plants this large being brought up from as deep as 150 m. That's deeper than the Great Pyramid of Giza is tall. These forests should be impossible. Like any other plant, kelps require light to grow. Yet these specimens grow as large as and often even larger than their shallow counterparts. All with less light than they should require just to stay alive. Then again, the mesophotic is the border between two worlds. One where life depends on the energy provided by sunlight, and another where life has learned to live in darkness. So, how have these large, light-dependent organisms >> >> adapted to thrive at such depths? Researchers are still investigating the answer to this question, but they do have theories. Mesophotic kelps photosynthesize more efficiently than their shallow counterparts, and some have suggested this might be due to having very large surface area relative to biomass, which allows deep kelps to maximize light harvesting and minimize respiration. By taking these adaptations into account, existing research still suggests that deep kelp forests don't photosynthesize enough to sustain their growth and respiration, even at peak sunlight. So, the real key to their success might be thriftiness. Photosynthesis is dependent on four main ingredients: sunlight, water, nutrients, and CO2. And while sunlight is severely limited, the deep ocean is full of water and nutrients. It's also full of CO2. However, most marine CO2 is in a bicarbonate form that requires lots of energy to convert. >> >> Most aquatic plants have evolved mechanisms to handle this energy-intensive process, but deep kelps take the easy way out. Since their deeper waters have more CO2, which doesn't need to be converted, they get their fill through low-energy passive diffusion. Mesophotic kelps also save energy by not having to produce molecular sunscreen, which plants typically need to avoid damage from excess sunlight. These aren't the only tricks deep kelps use to conserve energy. In the darker winter months, these plants suppress their respiration and subsist on the carbon reserves they stocked up over the summer. This adaptation is similar to how shallow polar kelp forests survive months of darkness. But while mesophotic kelp's access to sunlight also changes with the seasons, temperature is fairly consistent in the deep ocean. So, they don't have to contend with extreme temperature swings. This lets these forests act as a climate refuge, providing a stable home for species in shallower zones fleeing marine heat waves. Kelps also draw down some of the atmospheric CO2 that causes climate change. In fact, kelp detritus will keep photosynthesizing and drawing down CO2 as it drifts to the ocean floor. The researchers are still investigating its exact impact on the carbon cycle. There's still lots to be learned about the ocean's hidden forests. In fact, we still don't even know how much of the seafloor they cover. Since most kelp forests are invisible to satellites, researchers need to use cutting-edge underwater robots to find the answer. These remotely operated vehicles, ROVs, can explore and film depths far beyond the reach of humans. And with their help, marine biologists have already found new kelp forests, such as those off the tropical coast of the Galapagos Islands. 5ljV0Vxu00M.tx: You’re an astronaut orbiting 400 kilometers above Earth when suddenly an alert flashes across your display. The system responsible for producing the breathable air on board has failed. Now, you and your crewmates must work with mission control to identify the problem and fix it as quickly as possible. This might seem like a scene from a sci-fi thriller, but for astronauts on the International Space Station, dealing with situations like this is a reality of life. For over 25 years, ISS’s air supply systems have revolutionized space missions. Yet the need for regular maintenance, repairs, and upgrades has pushed engineers to develop even more reliable systems for future spacecraft. Creating breathable air in space has two requirements: supplying oxygen and removing exhaled carbon dioxide before it builds up. Every astronaut in space needs, on average, about 0.8 kilograms of oxygen a day. Most early space missions met this demand by storing oxygen on board in pressurized tanks. For example, the eight-day Apollo 11 mission to the moon carried three astronauts, along with around 50 kilograms of oxygen for life support— more than enough for the crew to survive on. Canisters containing lithium hydroxide would chemically react with carbon dioxide, scrubbing it from the cabin. But the launch of the first space station marked a turning point. For the first time, crews would remain in orbit for months, not days. A typical 6 to 8 month expedition with seven crew members might require over a thousand kilograms of oxygen, demanding about 30 large tanks. And constantly shipping this massive load to and from orbit would be expensive. So, engineers developed a solution: using water and a process called electrolysis, a system that makes oxygen directly onboard. Water is relatively easy to come by on the ISS thanks to its robust recovery system. It captures nearly all moisture onboard— from sweat, exhalation, wash water, and even urine— and purifies it into fresh, potable water. This clean water is routed to an electrolyzer, a device equipped with two electrodes, one positive and one negative. When an electric current is applied, the electrolyzer breaks down water molecules into oxygen and hydrogen gases. Oxygen collects near the positive electrode, and hydrogen gas bubbles form near the negative electrode. But there’s a problem— getting these gases out of the water. On Earth, bubbles naturally float to the top of denser liquids due to gravity. But in orbit, where everything is in freefall, bubbles tend to cling to the electrodes. One solution is to pump water through the electrolyzer, carrying the bubbles away to a separator. Here, the gas-filled water is spun much like a washing machine in its final spin cycle, forcing the liquid outward while the gas collects in the center. In the end, oxygen is released into the cabin. Hydrogen gas is either vented into space or routed to a reactor, where it combines with captured exhaled carbon dioxide to make methane and water. But this system isn't perfect. The process for separating bubbles from water relies on many complex moving parts that are prone to breaking or malfunctioning. And as space agencies set their sights on expeditions deeper into space, like year-long crewed trips to Mars, this approach becomes increasingly impractical. So, researchers are exploring new ways to separate out this gas. One promising solution is to spin the gas-filled water inside the electrolyzer using magnets. This system takes advantage of a fundamental property of how electrons and magnets interact. When negatively charged molecules move perpendicularly through a magnetic field, the field applies a force on the molecules called a Lorentz force. It pushes them sideways, at a right angle to both the electric and magnetic fields. So, by positioning the magnets and current path in just the right way, this Lorentz force can swirl the liquid, separating out the oxygen and hydrogen gases— no pump or separator needed. This Magnetohydrodynamic Oxygen Generation Assembly, or MOGA, has no moving parts, so it requires less maintenance and replacement hardware, freeing up space onboard and allowing astronauts to spend more time on other endeavors. MOGA is still in the research phase, but it holds promise. With a more robust oxygen system, astronauts on future space stations and deep-space missions should be able to breathe a little easier.

DbEZmLoGDbk.tx: Losing a loved one can be one of the most traumatic experiences of a person’s life. Grief brings on a whole host of strong emotions that impact both our mental and physical health. But is it possible for these powerful feelings to endanger your life? In other words, can you actually die from a broken heart? One of the most widely documented medical phenomena addressing this question is the widowhood effect. Studies of elderly couples have found that a person’s risk of dying can increase by up to 90% over the three months following their spouse’s death, leading a significant number of couples to pass away months, weeks, or even days apart. There are a lot of theories explaining this effect. One study found that severe grief and depression were associated with higher levels of inflammatory proteins in the blood, potentially impairing the immune system. And depression, combined with the loss of a supporting partner, can make it hard for a person to keep up with their daily health needs. Similarly, chronic stress can alter hormone levels, impair digestion, and dysregulate the immune system. But while all these factors can reduce life expectancy, there’s another condition where powerful emotions can directly endanger someone’s life: takotsubo cardiomyopathy. Also known as stress cardiomyopathy, or “broken heart syndrome,” this was originally labeled by Japanese doctors in 1990, who named the condition after the Japanese word for an octopus trap. In takotsubo cardiomyopathy, the left ventricle— one of the heart’s four chambers— pools with blood and balloons outward, giving it a distinctively takotsubo-like shape. And while most patients can recover over several weeks, roughly 5% will experience a potentially lethal cardiac arrest. While the exact cause of takotsubo cardiomyopathy is still being studied, the condition often appears after a sudden traumatic event. And since cases have been triggered by both shocking grief and unexpected happiness, it's likely not the nature of the emotion that matters, but the intensity. Intense emotional events lead to a sudden increase in two hormones: epinephrine, also known as adrenaline, and norepinephrine. Both these hormones interact with beta-adrenergic receptors, which have a high concentration in the left ventricle. So during takotsubo cardiomyopathy, researchers believe epinephrine and norepinephrine flood the left ventricle, triggering it to contract rapidly and repeatedly. Within minutes, this activity exhausts the ventricle. And since it’s unable to pump effectively, blood begins to pool. This hormonal spike can also cause spasms in the blood vessels that supply the heart with oxygen and nutrients. So despite all the blood inside the heart, the muscle tissue itself may not be getting enough blood flow to function. The result of all this is something that often feels like a heart attack without actually being one. People undergoing takotsubo cardiomyopathy often experience intense chest pain and shortness of breath, even though their arteries aren’t blocked like they would be during a heart attack. This similarity in symptoms also makes the condition difficult to diagnose, and it's easily confused for more common cardiac conditions. Fortunately, the initial treatment for takotsubo cardiomyopathy and a heart attack is the same. Doctors may prescribe blood thinners to prevent clotting in the heart and beta blockers to slow the heart's contractions. Beyond that, patients might take blood thinners and blood pressure medications to protect their heart in the long run. But there currently aren’t any specific treatments for takotsubo cardiomyopathy. We also don't know exactly when it will strike. The population that appears most at risk is postmenopausal women, perhaps because estrogen helps prevent cardiovascular disease, and menopause decreases estrogen production. But obviously anyone can experience traumatic emotions. The good news is that in most cases patients make a full recovery. Because while our bodies are sensitive to the ups and downs of our emotions, they're also resilient. And much like a broken bone, even a broken heart can heal with time and care.

HDt_rTPPh70.tx: Of the many bewildering behaviors cats display, one of the strangest is their obsession with a specific species of plant. After just one whiff, even the most stoic cat can start pawing, drooling, biting, and wriggling in a state of pure feline euphoria. So, why do cats go crazy for catnip? This is the question cat behavior expert Masao Miyazaki and chemist Toshio Nishikawa set out to answer in 2013. Along with their research teams from Iwate and Nagoya University, they began by studying silvervine— a plant that sparks a similar response to catnip. First, the researchers painstakingly extracted chemical compounds from the plant and dribbled various combinations of them onto filter papers. Then they brought in some cats and studied which compounds they were drawn to. Overwhelmingly, their feline testers pounced on the papers containing nepetalactol. And when Miyazaki and his student Reiko Uenoyama ran blood tests on the cats who’d interacted with nepetalactol, they found their systems were flooded with endorphins. These hormones block pain signals, relieve stress, and generally create a happy, calming effect. And catnip triggers the same endorphin rush with a similar chemical called nepetalactone, and it’s this flood of happy hormones that gives catnip and silvervine their signature drug-like response. These compounds don't just trigger this effect in small cats. When the researchers brought nepetalactol-treated filter papers to a few zoos, leopards, lynxes, and jaguars all dove face first into the compound. This was big news. If all these different cat species reacted to nepetalactol in the same way, the response was very likely a shared evolutionary trait— potentially something important to cat survival that stretched back millions of years. When the silvervine researchers presented their work at a conference, one evolutionary biologist raised a compelling theory. In chemical terms, both nepetalactol and nepetalactone are classified as an iridoid— a type of natural compound known to contain insect-repelling properties. So perhaps cats rubbing their faces in silvervine and catnip were applying an ancient form of bug spray. To test this, researchers set up cages of mosquitoes that cats could stick their heads into. And sure enough, the cats that had been treated with nepetalactol got fewer mosquito bites than the cats in the control group. The same effect was true for the scientists who’d volunteered their arms in solidarity with their feline subjects. These mosquito-repelling properties are currently our best explanation for why cats love silvervine and catnip. But researchers still had one more question: in their state of euphoria, cats tend to vigorously bite, lick, and rub against these plants. But do cats really need to go this crazy to get their bug repelling effects? To investigate rubbing, they provided cats with filter papers treated with microscopic amounts of nepetalactol. And sure enough, even these tiny doses made the papers irresistible, suggesting that microscopic amounts of bug repellent can be transferred by rubbing alone. As for biting and licking, the researchers found that when cats damage the plant, the leaves actually produce more mosquito-repellent chemicals. So your cat isn’t just ripping open their bags of catnip to be annoying, their evolutionary instincts are just trying to get even more of that bug protection. Cats are far from the only animal to use natural plants for purposes like this. Apes swallow scratchy and hairy leaves to dislodge parasites from their guts. Sheep munch on tannin-rich plants to kill intestinal worms, and monarch butterflies use toxic milkweed to kill parasites that normally impair their flight. Just like cats’ ability to find mosquito repellent, these behaviors can help humans identify useful plants and ingredients in the natural world. So, the next time you see your feline friend on catnip binge, don’t worry— it’s only medicinal.

aob7rM5PV5A.tx: The year is 100 CE, and 11-year-old Julia Lucilla is playing with her ivory doll Pompeia. Named after the Roman Emperor Trajan’s wife, Pompeia is only 20 centimeters tall, with joints at her arms, legs, knees, and elbows, and a bevy of miniature clothes and accessories. With her doll in hand, Julia hosts elaborate dinner parties, helps Aeneas escape Troy, and accompanies her father on work trips to Egypt. This ancient scene is likely familiar to any modern parent, and that’s because kids have been going on imaginary adventures with their toys for thousands of years. While the most common ancient playthings would likely have been sticks and rocks, evidence of their use for play is archaeologically invisible. However, archaeologists have found material, visual, and written evidence for toys across the ancient world. In Anatolia circa 3000 BCE, miniature toy carriages raced through the dirt at the hands of energetic youngsters. A thousand years later, in the Indus Valley, a toddler giggled gleefully at the chirping sound created by their dove-shaped terracotta whistle. Alongside whistles and wheeled toys, dolls are another common ancient plaything, though they can be a little harder to identify. While some archaeologists think ancient female figurines found across Afro-Eurasia may have been children’s toys, others believe them to be sacred fertility idols. But we do know dolls like Pompeia were popular in Greece and Rome, with hair and clothes designed to reflect changing adult fashions. And thousands of years later in the Arctic, Inuit children carried fur-clad dolls carved of wood or walrus tusk. But perhaps the most common ancient toy is the humble ball. Thousands of years ago, children in ancient Egypt, China, Greece, and Mesoamerica kicked and threw balls made of everything from leather and linen to papyrus and palm fiber. The rules for most of their games have been lost to time, however some kids may have imitated adult games we know more about. For example, ancient Greek children might have played episkuros, a team sport where players competed to push their opponents outside the pitch by hurling the ball as far as possible. Meanwhile, Mesoamerican kids might have played a game where players try to hit a rubber ball through a hoop using only their hips. Then again, in some cultures, this game had religious significance, so it's possible those children steered clear of this sacred sport. In any case, rougher, physical play was often limited by ancient gender expectations, with young girls being left out of rowdier ball games in Rome and Egypt. Spartan girls circa 400 BCE did engage in the same rigorous physical activities as boys, but largely because adults believed it would strengthen their bodies for childbearing. Fortunately, this wasn’t the only reason ancient adults encouraged kids to play. Athenian philosopher Plato observed that toys like building blocks and miniature farming implements were useful tools for learning the skills needed in adulthood. That said, many ancient cultures expected children to give up their games and toys as they grew up. A common Roman phrase described a child “giving up nuts” when taking up their adult responsibilities since nuts were used in a variety of simple games. And young Roman girls left their dolls as offerings to the gods as part of preparing for their wedding. However, other childhood games resembled those men and women continued to enjoy into adulthood. One, called knucklebones, was popular across the ancient Mediterranean. Usually crafted from the ankle bones of sheep or pigs, they could be used as jacks or dice, with different faces earning different point values. In addition to games of chance, ancient adults played a variety of strategic board games, which may have been introduced during childhood. Some particularly well-recorded examples include the Royal Game of Ur in ancient Mesopotamia, Go in China, Senet in Egypt, and Ludus latrunculorum— or, the Game of Soldiers— in Rome. Today, playful kids follow the same instincts as their ancient ancestors. They continue to make up ball games, invent stories for their favorite dolls, and send toy cars skittering across the floor. Because the simplest kinds of play never get old.

You can say, “I appreciate this” or “I really appreciate this” or even “You’re a lifesaver.” “You’re a lifesaver” is a good expression to use when someone does you a favor: this can be a coworker or a friend. “You’re a lifesaver.” But let’s say one of your … favor for you. For example, they took care of your dog while you were traveling. In a situation like that, you can say, “Thank you so much for taking care of my dog.” Or, because it’s a favor, you might want to then return the favor one day. In that case, you can say, “I owe you one.” “I owe you one” means you want to do a favor in return one day. Well, this is a long sentence, so that combined with the “I would like” and “heartfelt gratitude” and “express”? Very formal. Now, before we finish, I want to share with you the secret sauce … like a native speaker. If you’ve listened to my podcast for a while, you know I say this often: tone matters. You can say the most formal sentence and sound awful if you’re using a flat, bored tone, like this: “I would like to express my heartfelt gratitude.” See what I mean? So be aware of your tone.
